A genuine Rekor v2 entry whose verifier is a certificate — the v3 shape,
complete, and verifiable end to end.

Published 2026-08-16 to https://log2025-1.rekor.sigstore.dev (HTTP 201
Created, logIndex 67966366). Nothing in this repository authored the log's
half of any of it: not the checkpoint, not its signature lines, not the tree
the audit path walks.

This entry replaces an earlier one (logIndex 67766084) that was identical in
shape but carried the old `https://synchronicity.dev/zone-key/v1` predicate
type. A Statement is committed to the log by digest, so a predicate type
cannot be edited after the fact — changing it meant publishing again. The old
entry is still in the log and still valid on its own terms; it simply no
longer matches what this build produces.

  statement.json           471 B  the in-toto Statement, byte-exact — the
                                  DSSE PAE preimage the leaf's digest commits
                                  to. Keeping it is what makes this fixture
                                  total (see "what this proves").
  certificate.der          945 B  the entry's verifier, extracted from
                                  spec.hashedRekordV002.signature.verifier
                                    .x509Certificate.rawBytes.
  canonicalized_body.json 1631 B  the Merkle leaf preimage, verbatim, as the
                                  log returned it.
  checkpoint.txt           643 B  the signed note at tree size 67 966 402.
                                  It carries FOUR signature lines: the log's
                                  own Ed25519 signature plus three witness
                                  cosignatures. This design does not interpret
                                  cosignatures at all, but the parser has to
                                  tolerate them — narrowing it to a single
                                  signature would reject every checkpoint the
                                  production log serves, and this file is the
                                  regression test for that.
  proof.bin               3275 B  the encoded RekorProof v3 record — the
                                  exact bytes a zone serves at
                                  _synchronicity-rekor.<apex>, carrying 15
                                  audit-path hops.
  anchor.txt               144 B  the DNSSEC trust anchor this zone is under.
  log_index.txt                   67966366.

The entry is a `rollover` for zone-key-transparency.demo.invalid, key tag
27337. Its chain verifies and covers that key, so a monitor holding the anchor
below classifies it tier A — an authorization — and reports it the first time
it sees it. That is what crates/synch-monitor/tests/real_entry.rs asserts.

THIS ENTRY PREDATES THE REMOVAL OF THE SUCCESSION COUNTERSIGNATURE

When these bytes were published the design had a second custom extension,
2.25.1138370866, carrying a countersignature by the previous zone key (here,
key tag 17123) — and a three-tier monitor that used it to separate a rotation
from a substitution. Both are gone: an attacker who has taken the registrar
holds the DS and can always build a valid chain, so the countersignature was
doing the whole job of that distinction, and without it the monitor stopped
attempting the distinction rather than attempting it badly. It now reports
every newly authorized key and leaves the operator's own records to say which
ones they caused.

**This did not require a new log entry, and must not be given one.** A Merkle
leaf is immutable, so the extension is still in these bytes and always will
be. Nothing reads it. The certificate parser collects extensions and looks
them up by OID, and refuses nothing for carrying one it has no name for
(crates/synch-net/src/x509.rs), so the entry verifies exactly as it did
before — the extension is simply vestigial. That is asserted rather than
assumed, in two places that name the OID directly: the extension's continued
presence and irrelevance in crates/synch-monitor/tests/real_entry.rs, and the
same over the client verifier in crates/synch-net/tests/rekor_zone_key.rs.
The certificate is still 945 bytes for the same reason: shrinking it would
mean minting a second leaf for a claim already in the log.

The arc 2.25.1138370866 is therefore **burned**. Do not reuse it for a new
meaning — this entry, and any other published in that window, would decode
under the new one.

WHAT THIS PROVES, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT

It proves interoperability with the real log: that Rekor v2 accepts a
self-signed certificate as a hashedrekord verifier with no chain validation of
any kind, that a 945-byte certificate carrying custom extensions under the
narrowed 2.25 arcs is accepted, that the returned inclusion proof and
checkpoint verify under the log key this build embeds, and that the whole
record round-trips through the wire form a zone actually serves.

It does NOT prove real-world DNSSEC chain validation. The chain in this
certificate is SELF-ANCHORED: the apex is its own trust anchor, because no
DNSSEC-signed domain was available to publish under, and minting a certificate
naming a domain we do not control would be squatting a name in a permanent
public log. A monitor anchored at the ICANN root therefore classifies this
entry tier C, correctly — it cannot tell whether the key was authorized.
ICANN-rooted validation is the job of the separate fixture in
../dnssec_chain/, captured from live DNS for cloudflare.com, which exercises
RSASHA256 at the root and ECDSAP256SHA256 below it.

REGENERATING

Publishing is a permanent, public, irreversible write. Do it only when the
entry format changes in a way that invalidates these bytes, and keep the SAN
under .invalid so no real name is claimed. Afterwards the pinned constants in
crates/synch-net/tests/rekor_zone_key.rs (LOG_INDEX, KEY_TAG, tree size,
certificate length) and crates/synch-monitor/tests/real_entry.rs (LOG_INDEX,
key tag, DS prefix) all have to move with it. A regenerated entry will NOT
carry 2.25.1138370866, so the two tests that assert the vestigial extension is
present should be deleted rather than updated — they exist to prove the
removal needed no republish, and a republished fixture has nothing to prove.
